pages.text: A signal reaches another station two ways:$(li)$(thing)Line of sight$(): out to a range set by the band (VHF about 500 blocks), fading with distance.$(li)$(thing)Skip$(): HF bounces off the sky and comes down far away, in a window of distances that differs by band and between day and night. In between is a silent zone.

Rules of thumb: 80 and 40 m are best at night, 20 m by day, 10 m only opens when the sun is lively.$(br2)$(thing)/bandcalculate <from> <to>$() estimates every band between two points under the current conditions.
pages.title: Which band?
Commercial bands
pages.text: Besides the ham bands there are two commercial ones. $(thing)Low band$() (30-50 MHz) sits between 10 m and VHF: by line of sight it reaches further than 2 m but not quite as far as 10 m, and like 10 m it only skips by day when the sun is lively, never at night. $(thing)Commercial VHF$() (150-174 MHz, with the marine channels) travels like 2 m. See the $(l:radiocraft:propagation/band_plan)Band Plan$() for who uses what.
Being a few kHz off still lets you hear SSB, sounding higher or lower and thinner; 11 kHz off, nothing. FM is heard up to 2 kHz off.
pages.title: Off frequency

pages.text: Hills in the way weaken line of sight: badly on VHF, much less on 80 m, and HF also loses some at every cliff. Skip leaves at a low angle on 10 and 20 m, so a station deep in a valley loses it over the valley walls, while 80 m goes nearly straight up. A handheld indoors or underground is weaker. RF passes through wood planks, stairs and slabs, glass, wool and leaves, so an antenna in the attic does fine. Build high!
pages.title: Hills and valleys
